idiom_name: Selector + SelectionKey loop with attachments as handlers
implementation_notes: java.nio provides the whole synchronous-event-demultiplexer role in the JDK: select()/select(timeout) block until a registered channel is ready and add the corresponding SelectionKey to the selected-key set, the key carries the channel plus its interest and ready operations, and attachment() is where the per-connection handler or session is stored - so the initiation dispatcher is a few dozen lines around keys() and selectedKeys(). The Javadoc also fixes the loop's concurrency rules: a selector and its key set are safe for several threads but the selected-key set is not, so one thread owns the loop and other threads change interest through wakeup(). Hand-write this loop for dependency-free gateways or to understand a framework; in production the same structure is usually Netty's.
pitfalls: Forgetting selectedKeys().clear() leaves the keys in the ready set, so select() returns at once on every iteration and the loop spins at 100% CPU.
A blocking call in the handler (JDBC, file I/O, a slow parse) stalls every channel on the selector; that is the reactor's cardinal sin and the JVM gives no warning.
An accepted SocketChannel is blocking by default and must be set non-blocking before register(), and a cancelled key is deregistered only by a later selection operation, so cleanup lags cancellation.
Registration or interest changes from another thread need Selector.wakeup(), and the selected-key set together with its fail-fast iterator must not be touched off the loop thread.

variants.name: Netty NioEventLoop with a ChannelPipeline (framework realization)
variants.implementation_notes: Netty packages the pattern: NioEventLoop is documented as a SingleThreadEventLoop implementation that registers the channels with a Selector and does the multiplexing of these in the event loop, one selector per loop thread, while EventLoopGroup spreads channels across those loops. The initiation dispatcher (the loop), the registry (channel-to-loop assignment plus the ChannelPipeline) and the rearm/dispatch protocol are framework concerns, so application code only implements ChannelHandler classes. Choose Netty over a hand-written selector loop whenever more than one core is needed, when a protocol stack should be reused, or when the loop must be shared by many services; keep the JDK loop for trivial dependency-free cases.
pitfalls: Running blocking code in a ChannelHandler blocks that event loop and every channel assigned to it; offload to a DefaultEventExecutorGroup or a business thread pool.
Channel state may only be mutated on its event loop; touching it from another thread needs channel.eventLoop().execute(...) or a promise, otherwise the change races the dispatch.
One loop per thread is not free: creating many NioEventLoopGroups (or a loop per connection) multiplies selectors and threads; size groups like core pools and share them.
